summary: NASA and SpaceX successfully launched four astronauts to the International Space Station aboard the Crew-13 mission, marking the day's primary operational launch. In military and civil space developments, the White House nominated a new commander to lead U.S. Space Command as the U.S. Space Force retired a 1970s-era missile warning satellite constellation, selected two companies to build new space-to-space satellites by 2028, and received calls in a new report to adopt laser communications to ease data bottlenecks. Meanwhile, the Department of Defense awarded a demonstration contract for space-based solar power beaming, and defense leadership announced plans to create a new Autonomous Warfare Command. Internationally, China launched its Guowang and Yaogan-40 satellites to begin a busy fourth-quarter launch manifest, while Latvia's LMT Group partnered with Novaspace to develop a regional 5G/6G satellite communications strategy. Commercial activity accelerated as Varda raised $251 million in Series D funding, Satlyt secured $8 million following Transporter-18 orbital data center testing, and Quantum Space executed a launch processing agreement with All Points Logistics. In space science and medicine, NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided new observations of planet-shattering collisions, while researchers found that spaceflights exceeding 90 days are associated with increased rates of astronaut hip fractures. Looking ahead, skywatchers should monitor the early October skies for a rare lunar occultation of Jupiter alongside Saturn reaching opposition.
